summary: Following a November 15, 2023 mandate, schools in the Silicon Valley region are preparing to fully integrate coding and computational thinking into curricula by the next academic year, framed as both educational reform and an economic strategy. The note covers the economic case for coding literacy, the shift from consuming to creating technology, challenges such as teacher training and the digital divide, and industry and community partnerships. Other states and countries are watching and may follow if it succeeds.
one_line: Silicon Valley-area schools, under a November 2023 mandate, are integrating coding and computational thinking into curricula as an educational and economic strategy.
key_facts: A mandate issued on November 15, 2023 requires schools across the state to fully integrate coding and computational thinking into curricula by the start of the next academic year.
Dr. Amelia Richardson of the University of California says "coding is the literacy of the 21st century" in a paper dated December 8, 2023.
According to tech recruitment firm HiredTech, jobs requiring coding skills are growing 50% faster than the market overall.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects a 13% increase in employment in computer and information technology occupations by 2030, outpacing the average for all occupations.
Maxine Thompson, a curriculum specialist at the Department of Education, said on January 23, 2024 that children should learn "not just to consume technology but to understand and control it."
An initiative launched September 1, 2023 partners with universities and private coding bootcamps to fast-track upskilling of teachers.
Jane Park, a local education advocate, warns of a "digital divide" that could leave behind students from less affluent backgrounds; schools are seeking funding for digital tools and resources.
The new curriculum emphasizes hands-on, project-based, "minds-on" learning with tangible coding projects.
Schools are partnering with local startups and established tech giants for internships and co-created curricular materials.
Bob Marino, founder of the non-profit CodeFuture, says community after-school programs and weekend workshops are invaluable for continuing momentum.
Thom Walters, a Silicon Valley economic analyst, says failing to prepare the workforce risks falling behind on the global stage.
Other states and countries are watching the experiment, and success could realign global educational standards.
